title: The Sleeping House
premise: Folklorist Hazel Ravensworth arrives at the village of Marrowfen to record a lullaby the locals refuse to sing twice, staying at Ravensworth House — a home she slowly realizes belonged to a family she has no memory of, yet whose photographs include her face. As every mirror in the house begins reflecting one second late, Hazel discovers the house is counting its family, and the well beneath it refills each generation to take them. To survive, she must convince the house's lingering dead — the found family she never knew she had — to leave before the count completes, ending with Hazel singing the lullaby a second time to break the count and letting the house finally sleep empty.
about_author: Jonah Oyelaran is a Nigerian-British writer who grew up between Lagos and a Yorkshire mill town, collecting his grandmother's lullabies and his neighbors' ghost stories with equal seriousness. He writes horror about the places that mistake memory for ownership.

chapters.title: The Song They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She arrives in Marrowfen to record the village's forbidden lullaby; an old woman hums half of it and stops, terrified. Hazel takes lodging at Ravensworth House, her only affordable option. The emotional beat is uneasy curiosity — she feels strangely at home in a place she's never seen.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She settles in, keeping her folklorist's habits: lights on, doors counted each night — eleven doors, always eleven. She finds a child's chalk tally on a pantry wall, decades old, still being added to. The beat is creeping wrongness beneath domestic comfort.

chapters.title: The Photograph with Her Face
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the attic she finds a 1970s family portrait: a mother, father, three children — and a young woman who is unmistakably Hazel. No one in the village will discuss the Ravensworths. The beat is vertigo; her sense of identity begins to crack.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room a full second behind her movements — including reflections of things she hasn't done yet. She smashes the hallway glass; it re-forms overnight. The beat is dread made intimate.

chapters.title: The Well Beneath the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, shifting to the mother, Edith Ravensworth, in 1974. Edith heard the well refilling under the floorboards and counted the family — five — aloud to keep them safe. Hazel reads Edith's diary in parallel, learning the house counts its family and takes what it counts. The beat is inherited fear.

chapters.title: The Family in the Walls
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The house's dead begin appearing in the late reflections: Edith, the father Thomas, three children. They are not hostile — they are waiting for her, setting her place at dinner in the mirrored world. The beat is uncanny warmth; horror and belonging tangled together.

chapters.title: What the Village Buried
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She confronts the old woman from chapter one, who confesses: the Ravensworths were taken by the well in '74, and the village sang the lullaby twice at their funeral — which is why no one sings it twice anymore. The second singing wakes the count. The beat is guilty communal memory.

chapters.title: Hazel, Counted
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The tally on the pantry wall now includes her: six. The mirrors show her reflection staying behind when she leaves the room. She realizes the house believes she is the lost fourth child, returned. The beat is the seduction of belonging — she wants to be counted.

chapters.title: Edith's Lullaby
chapters.summary: Alternating Hazel and Edith POVs. Edith wrote the lullaby not to soothe her children but to teach them the count — each verse a number, a door, a name. Hazel learns the song's true function: sung once, it lulls the house; sung twice, it wakes the well. The beat is revelation.

chapters.title: The Refill
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Water rises in the well shaft beneath the kitchen; the taps run warm; the house hums the lullaby on its own. The dead children appear at her bedroom door asking her to come downstairs where it's safe. The beat is rising panic and maternal tenderness she can't refuse.

chapters.title: Downstairs, Where It's Safe
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She follows the children to the kitchen, nearly stepping into the open well, and is saved by Edith's reflection grabbing her wrist from the mirror — the dead mother protecting her from the house's hunger. The beat is the first proof the family loves her more than the house does.

chapters.title: The Fourth Child
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, 1974, final entry. The fourth child, Rose, died before the count began; Edith counted her anyway, and the house, cheated of one, has been waiting for Rose to come home ever since. Hazel understands: she isn't Rose — but the house doesn't care. The beat is grief reframed as appetite.

chapters.title: Leaving Is Dying
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The dead explain their trap: the house keeps them because they were counted, and the counted cannot leave — the well refills to collect them each generation. They have been trying to get out for fifty years. The beat is despair with a spark of alliance.

chapters.title: The Un-counting
chapters.summary: Hazel and Edith's POVs converge. Edith proposes the forbidden act: sing the lullaby a second time, deliberately — but backwards, verse by verse, un-counting each name. It might free the family or wake the well early. The beat is terrible hope.

chapters.title: The Village Refuses
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She begs the village to sing with her — the un-counting needs voices that knew the Ravensworths. They refuse, lock their doors, and one man tries to burn the house down with her inside. The beat is isolation sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Six Voices
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. With no village, the family itself must be the chorus: Hazel plus the five dead, six voices for six names. They rehearse in the mirrored world, where the reflections now move with them, no longer late — the house is listening. The beat is found family forged in rehearsal.

chapters.title: The Well Fills
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The well brims; water climbs the walls; the house begins the count aloud — five, four — collecting the children first. Hazel sings the first verse backwards as the youngest boy dissolves into her arms. The beat is the climax's first blow: loss even in resistance.

chapters.title: The Second Singing
chapters.summary: Hazel and Edith's POVs, fully merged. In the flooded kitchen, Hazel and Edith sing the lullaby's second half backwards, un-naming Thomas and the children while the well pulls at them. Hazel offers her own name last — choosing to be un-counted, giving up the belonging she finally found. The beat is sacrificial love.

chapters.title: Rose
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, in the moment between. The house, offered Hazel's name, hesitates — and Edith instead gives it the name it was always owed: Rose. The count completes on the child who was already gone, and the debt closes. The beat is a mother's final arithmetic of grief.

chapters.title: The House Sleeps
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The water drains; the mirrors go dark, then ordinary; the tally on the pantry wall fades to nothing. The family is released — Edith's last reflection presses a hand to the glass in farewell. The beat is mourning and peace intertwined.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, Ten Names
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She records the lullaby once, never twice, and leaves it with the village archive along with the Ravensworths' true story. The old woman sings it with her — once — the first time the village has honored the dead instead of fearing them. The beat is communal repair.

chapters.title: What Belongs to Her
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, epilogue. Months later, Hazel keeps the lights on and the doors counted out of habit, not fear, in her own small flat — where a single mirror sometimes lags a half-second, and she waves at it anyway. The beat is quiet resolution: identity chosen, family carried, belonging made rather than inherited.
